title: Where is your money right now?
principle: Stock and credit are cash you can't spend. Limit both.

screens.text: Let me start with a story from Uttar Pradesh. A sugarcane farmer, Piyush Kumar, sold his crop to a sugar mill. By May 2019, the mill owed him ₹80,000. The law says a mill that pays after 14 days must add interest. By September, he still had not been paid.

screens.prompt: He had sold his whole crop. What problem do you think four months without payment caused?

options.label: Not much. The money was safe
His own bills still had to be paid

screens.why: His own bills still had to be paid. Piyush owed more than ₹1 lakh on a bank loan, and the bank sent him a notice. He had sold his crop but had no cash to pay. He told a reporter he no longer grows cane on his 30 acres.

screens.title: Earned, but not paid
screens.text: Piyush had earned his ₹80,000, but he had not received it. His own bills still had to be paid. He was not alone. In September 2019, UP's mills owed cane farmers ₹6,480 crore for cane they had already grown and sold.

screens.title: How long your cash is away
screens.text: You pay your supplier first. Your money then sits on your shelf as stock. After you sell, it may wait until the customer pays you. These days are your cash conversion cycle. If your supplier lets you pay later, your cash stays with you longer.

screens.prompt: You buy goods today, sell them 20 days later, and get paid 30 days after that. How many days is your money gone?
screens.why: Exactly. Your goods sit on the shelf for 20 days, then you wait 30 more days for payment. So 20 + 30 = 50 days. That's your cash conversion cycle.

wrong.a: That's only the 20 days your goods stay on the shelf. After the sale, you wait 30 more days for payment. So 20 + 30 = 50 days.
wrong.b: I see what you did: you counted only the 30 days after the sale. Add the 20 days before the sale. That makes 50 days.

screens.prompt: The mill kept Piyush waiting for four months, not 14 days. Who really paid for this delay?

options.label: Nobody. The money was coming anyway

screens.why: Right. The mill kept his ₹80,000, while his own loan kept charging interest. Remember this: when a customer pays late, they are using your money. If you borrow money while waiting, you pay the interest.

wrong.a: The law says the mill should pay interest, but farmers were not getting it. Piyush's own loan still charged interest, so he paid for the delay.
wrong.c: The money was expected, but late payment still caused a cost. While Piyush waited, his loan charged interest and the bank sent him a notice.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: You do not have to grow cane to face this problem. When you sell on credit, customers keep your money until they pay. Imagine you run a small printing press that sells letterheads and visiting cards to offices.

screens.prompt: Offices order ₹20,000 of printing from you each day and pay 60 days later. How much money are you waiting to receive?
screens.why: Well done. Each day adds ₹20,000 of unpaid bills, and each bill stays unpaid for 60 days. So ₹20,000 × 60 = ₹12 lakh is unpaid at any time. You have earned this money but cannot use it yet.

wrong.a: I see what you did: there is a mistake in the zeros. ₹20,000 × 60 is ₹12,00,000, which is ₹12 lakh.
wrong.b: That's 30 days of unpaid bills. Your customers take 60 days to pay. So ₹20,000 × 60 = ₹12 lakh is unpaid.

screens.prompt: Offices order ₹20,000 a day. If they pay in 30 days, not 60, how much extra cash do you get sooner?
screens.why: Exactly. At 30 days, ₹20,000 × 30 = ₹6 lakh stays unpaid. Before, ₹12 lakh stayed unpaid, so you get ₹6 lakh sooner. If you would borrow that ₹6 lakh at 12% a year, you save ₹72,000 a year.

wrong.b: Multiply daily sales by the number of days: ₹20,000 × 30 = ₹6 lakh stays unpaid. Before, ₹12 lakh stayed unpaid. So you get ₹6 lakh sooner.
wrong.c: Not all of it. Customers still take 30 days to pay, so ₹6 lakh stays unpaid. You get the other ₹6 lakh sooner.

screens.prompt: You keep ₹4 lakh of paper and use ₹10,000 a day. Keep just 8 days of it. How much cash do you get back?
screens.why: Well done. ₹4 lakh is 40 days of paper. 8 days needs 8 × ₹10,000 = ₹80,000. So ₹4,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹3,20,000 becomes free. Money spent on stock is money you cannot use for anything else.

wrong.a: ₹80,000 is the cost of the 8 days of paper you keep. Subtract it from the ₹4 lakh you have now. ₹3,20,000 becomes free.
wrong.c: I see what you did: you removed only one day's ₹10,000. But 8 days costs 8 × ₹10,000 = ₹80,000. So ₹3,20,000 becomes free.

screens.prompt: I'll show you seven changes for your press. For each one, tell me: does it give you cash sooner or make you wait longer?

items.text: Ask for 30% before starting big orders
Buy 3 months of paper to get a bulk discount
Let a new client pay after 90 days
Sell old stock for what you paid
Ask your paper supplier for 30 days to pay
Keep every paper type in every colour
Give 2% off if customers pay in 7 days

screens.why: Advances, faster payment, selling old stock and paying your supplier later all give you cash sooner. Long payment times and too much stock make you wait longer. But some changes have a cost. The 2% discount gives you cash sooner, but you earn 2% less.

screens.setup: Then you get a big order. A hotel group wants ₹10 lakh of menus, brochures and cards. They want to pay after 120 days. Paper and wages cost ₹7 lakh now, and you have ₹4 lakh.
screens.question: How can you take this order without your cash getting stuck for four months?

options.label: Take it and borrow the missing ₹3 lakh
options.outcome: You borrow ₹3 lakh and wait four months for payment. You cannot pay your paper supplier on time. Other jobs also slow down because you do not have enough cash to buy paper.
options.why: You had to spend ₹7 lakh on one order and wait four months for payment. You borrowed ₹3 lakh of it. Like Piyush, you paid interest while waiting for the buyer to pay.
options.better: First, ask for an advance and faster payment.

options.label: Take it: 40% paid first, the rest in 45 days
options.outcome: Their ₹4 lakh advance plus your ₹4 lakh covers the ₹7 lakh cost. The other ₹6 lakh arrives in 45 days instead of 120.
options.why: Well played. You used less of your own cash and waited fewer days for payment. If you're a registered micro or small business, the law also helps you: if a buyer pays after 45 days, it can't claim that cost against its tax until it pays.

options.label: Say no. The order is too big
options.outcome: Your cash stays safe, but you lose the chance to earn the ₹3 lakh profit this order could give you with better payment terms.
options.why: The order itself was fine. The payment terms caused the problem.
options.better: Ask to change the payment terms before saying no.

screens.text: Money that customers owe you is a ___ you give. The days you wait for your cash are your cash conversion ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Piyush had sold his crop and was owed ₹80,000. But while he waited for the mill to pay, his own loan kept growing. Know how many days you wait for your money, and try to reduce that time.

summary: Your cash conversion cycle is the days your money is away: on your shelf, then with customers, less the time suppliers give you.
Cash stuck = sales a day × days customers take to pay. It's a loan you give, with no interest.
Cut days of credit and days of stock, and cash comes home.

cards.front: What do you call the days from paying for stock to getting paid by customers?
cards.back: The cash conversion cycle. Sell ₹10,000 a day with 45 days of credit, and ₹10,000 × 45 = ₹4,50,000 is stuck.

cards.front: A big buyer wants 90 days. You're a small registered maker. Ask for:
cards.back: Buyers who pay small makers after 45 days lose a tax deduction until they pay.
